Bantu-speaking farmers move into Southern Africa
questions.expected: San hunter-gatherers live across Southern Africa,Khoikhoi herders begin keeping livestock,Bantu-speaking farmers move into Southern Africa,Mapungubwe kingdom rises (Grade 6 topic)
questions.memo: The big timeline: hunter-gatherers (oldest), then herders, then farmers, then kingdoms grow from those farming societies.

questions.question: What did the farmers MEAN by 'communal work parties'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What were communal work parties in early farming societies?
options: Groups of neighbours coming together to plough or harvest one family's fields
questions.expected: Groups of neighbours coming together to plough or harvest one family's fields
questions.memo: When one family's field needed work, the village turned up. Next time it would be another family. This co-operation made everyone safer.

questions.question: True or false: Children in early farming societies WORKED from a young age.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: children in early farming societies worked from a young age.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Children helped with herding, fetching water, scaring birds from crops. They contributed and learned the skills they'd need as adults.

questions.question: Why was CATTLE such an important measure of wealth?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why were cattle such an important measure of wealth in farming societies?
options: Cattle give milk, meat, hides; can be used for trade (and lobola); and they survive dry years
questions.expected: Cattle give milk, meat, hides; can be used for trade (and lobola); and they survive dry years
questions.memo: Cattle = a walking storage of value. They feed you, can be traded, and unlike maize they don't fail in one bad season — they multiply. Hence so important.

questions.question: True or false: Early farmers in Southern Africa already worked IRON before the Europeans arrived.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: early farmers in Southern Africa already worked iron long before the Europeans arrived.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Africans were making iron tools, weapons and farming implements over 1500 years BEFORE European ships reached Southern Africa. African societies were innovative on their own.

questions.question: Tell me ONE thing the first farmers brought to Southern Africa.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing the first Bantu-speaking farmers brought to Southern Africa.
questions.expected: They brought iron-working
questions.memo: Good answers: farming (crops), cattle and other livestock, iron-working, pottery, the idea of villages/homesteads, new languages. All real.

questions.question: Which Southern African LANGUAGES today come partly from Bantu speakers AND from Khoisan?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which Southern African languages today combine elements from Bantu speakers AND from Khoisan languages?
options: IsiZulu, isiXhosa and other Nguni languages — the clicks come from Khoisan
questions.expected: IsiZulu, isiXhosa and other Nguni languages — the clicks come from Khoisan
questions.memo: The clicks in isiXhosa and isiZulu (like the 'c', 'q', 'x' sounds) were borrowed from Khoisan languages — proof that these groups lived together and influenced each other.

questions.question: What does this topic teach us about African history?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the big lesson about African history from this topic?
options: Africans built innovative farming, metalworking and trading societies long before Europeans arrived
Africa was empty until Europeans came
questions.expected: Africans built innovative farming, metalworking and trading societies long before Europeans arrived
questions.memo: This is one of the most important lessons of the topic. African history is rich, ancient and innovative. The story did not start with European arrival.

SS.L5.HIS.T03.title: An ancient African society: Egypt
SS.L5.HIS.T03.description: Life in ancient Egypt — the Nile, pharaohs, pyramids, hieroglyphics, religion, medicine; Tutankhamen's tomb.
SS.L5.HIS.T03.recovery_strategy: Egypt was an early African civilisation. The Nile river made farming possible in the desert. Pharaohs ruled; pyramids were tombs; hieroglyphics were the writing.

questions.question: Which CONTINENT is Egypt on?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which continent is Egypt on?
questions.expected: Africa
questions.memo: Egypt is in the north-east of Africa. Ancient Egyptian civilisation is one of the world's oldest — and it's an AFRICAN civilisation.

questions.question: Which river made ancient Egypt possible?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which river made ancient Egypt possible?
questions.expected: The Nile
questions.memo: The Nile floods every year, bringing rich soil. Without the Nile, Egypt would be desert. Almost all ancient Egyptian life was within walking distance of the river.

questions.question: Who was a 'PHARAOH'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was a pharaoh?
options: The king (or queen) of ancient Egypt — treated as a god
questions.expected: The king (or queen) of ancient Egypt — treated as a god
questions.memo: Pharaohs were the highest rulers — political leaders AND religious figures. Their orders shaped Egypt for thousands of years.

questions.question: What were the PYRAMIDS built for?
questions.ruby_prompt: What were the Egyptian pyramids built for?
options: As tombs for pharaohs and important people
questions.expected: As tombs for pharaohs and important people
questions.memo: Pyramids were huge tombs. The Egyptians believed the pharaoh's body and soul needed to be preserved for the afterlife — hence the giant stone tombs.

questions.question: What is 'HIEROGLYPHICS'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is hieroglyphics?
options: Ancient Egyptian writing made of picture-signs
questions.expected: Ancient Egyptian writing made of picture-signs
questions.memo: Each hieroglyph stood for a sound, a syllable or a whole word. It was used for over 3000 years on temples, tombs and papyrus.

questions.question: True or false: The Egyptians believed in MANY gods.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the ancient Egyptians believed in many gods.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Egyptians had hundreds of gods — Ra (the sun), Isis (motherhood), Osiris (the afterlife), Anubis (death). Each had a role in everyday life.

questions.question: What is the SPHINX?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Sphinx?
options: A giant statue with a lion's body and a human head, built near the pyramids
questions.expected: A giant statue with a lion's body and a human head, built near the pyramids

questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Tutankhamen?
options: A young pharaoh whose tomb was found almost untouched in 1922

questions.question: Who DISCOVERED Tutankhamen's tomb?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who discovered Tutankhamen's tomb?
questions.expected: Howard Carter, a British archaeologist

questions.question: Why did the Egyptians MUMMIFY bodies?

They thought it would bring rain

questions.question: Put these in order — the social structure of ancient Egypt (TOP to BOTTOM).

questions.question: Why was the Nile's YEARLY FLOOD so important?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why was the Nile's yearly flood so important to Egypt?
options: It left rich, dark soil on the fields — perfect for growing crops

questions.memo: The annual flood was a gift. Egypt's whole calendar was built around it — flood season, planting season, harvest season.

questions.question: True or false: The Egyptians used MATHEMATICS and ASTRONOMY.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the Egyptians used mathematics and astronomy.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. They tracked the stars to predict the Nile flood, used geometry to build pyramids, and developed a calendar of 365 days.

questions.question: Egyptian DOCTORS were skilled at:

options: Diagnosing diseases, examining patients, knowing anatomy and treating injuries
questions.expected: Diagnosing diseases, examining patients, knowing anatomy and treating injuries

questions.question: True or false: Egyptian society lasted for thousands of years.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: ancient Egyptian society lasted for thousands of years.

questions.memo: True. Egyptian civilisation lasted over 3000 years — far longer than most countries that exist today. They were stable, organised and very innovative.

questions.question: Tell me ONE thing about ancient Egypt you find INTERESTING.

questions.memo: Good answers: pyramids, mummies, hieroglyphics, the Nile, pharaohs, gods, Tutankhamen's gold, advanced medicine. All real and valid.

questions.question: What does ancient Egypt teach us about AFRICAN history?

questions.question: Why are PROVINCIAL HERITAGE places important for ALL South Africans?

questions.question: Why might we PROTECT heritage sites?

questions.question: What does this topic teach about SOUTH AFRICAN identity?

Land in the middle of the country
questions.expected: The low, flat land along the coast (between the sea and the escarpment)
questions.memo: Coastal plain = the strip of low land near the sea. Durban, East London and Cape Town are all on or near the coastal plain.

questions.question: Which is SOUTH AFRICA's highest mountain range?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is South Africa's highest mountain range?
questions.expected: The Drakensberg (uKhahlamba)
questions.memo: The Drakensberg has the highest peaks in Southern Africa — Thabana Ntlenyana (in Lesotho) is over 3 400m above sea level.

questions.question: Which famous mountain is in CAPE TOWN?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which famous mountain is in Cape Town?
questions.expected: Table Mountain
questions.memo: Table Mountain has a flat top that looks like a table. It's part of the Cape Floral Region and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: Where do most rivers in South Africa BEGIN?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where do most South African rivers begin?
options: In the high mountains and plateau
questions.expected: In the high mountains and plateau
questions.memo: Rivers always flow from HIGH to LOW. They start in high ground where rain falls or snow melts, then flow downhill to the sea.

questions.question: What is a 'TRIBUTARY'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a tributary?
options: A smaller river that joins a bigger river
questions.expected: A smaller river that joins a bigger river
questions.memo: Like branches of a tree feeding the trunk. The Gariep (Orange) river has many tributaries that feed water into it from far around.

questions.question: What is the BIGGEST river in South Africa?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is South Africa's biggest (longest) river?
questions.expected: The Gariep (Orange) River
questions.memo: The Gariep flows from the Drakensberg in Lesotho all the way to the Atlantic at the Namibian border — about 2 200 km.

questions.question: What is a 'CATCHMENT AREA' of a river?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a river's catchment area?
options: All the land where rain that falls eventually flows into that river
The mouth of the river only
Only the city near the river
questions.expected: All the land where rain that falls eventually flows into that river
questions.memo: Every river has a catchment — the area where rain flows into it. Damage in the catchment (pollution, deforestation) affects the river.

questions.question: What is the 'KAROO'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Karoo?
options: A large, dry, mostly flat region in central South Africa
questions.expected: A large, dry, mostly flat region in central South Africa
questions.memo: The Great Karoo and Little Karoo together cover huge areas. Very dry, sparse plants, sheep farms, fascinating fossils. A unique South African landscape.

questions.question: What is the 'HIGHVELD'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Highveld?
options: A high, mostly flat grassland area in central South Africa (Gauteng, Free State)
questions.expected: A high, mostly flat grassland area in central South Africa (Gauteng, Free State)
questions.memo: Highveld = high field. Cold winters, hot wet summers, big skies, lots of grass. Most of SA's gold mines are on the Highveld.

questions.question: What is the 'LOWVELD'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Lowveld?
options: A lower, hotter region in eastern South Africa — includes Kruger National Park
questions.expected: A lower, hotter region in eastern South Africa — includes Kruger National Park
questions.memo: Lowveld = low ground east of the escarpment. Hotter and more humid than the Highveld. The Kruger and Mpumalanga's wildlife areas are here.

questions.question: What is AUGRABIES FALLS?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is Augrabies Falls?
options: A famous waterfall on the Gariep River in the Northern Cape
questions.expected: A famous waterfall on the Gariep River in the Northern Cape
questions.memo: Augrabies is one of South Africa's most dramatic waterfalls — when the Gariep is full, water thunders down the gorge.

questions.question: Put these in order — a river's JOURNEY.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order — a river's journey from start to sea.
options: Small streams form and join into bigger rivers
The river flows across the land
The river reaches the sea at the coast
questions.expected: Rain falls in high mountains,Small streams form and join into bigger rivers,The river flows across the land,The river reaches the sea at the coast
questions.memo: Every river follows this path. Understand this and you understand how water shapes the land.

questions.question: How can BUILDING A DAM change the physical environment?
questions.ruby_prompt: How can building a dam change the physical environment?
options: It floods the area behind the wall, changing the river and what lives nearby
It moves the river to the sea
questions.expected: It floods the area behind the wall, changing the river and what lives nearby
questions.memo: Dams create huge man-made lakes. This drowns trees, displaces wildlife, sometimes displaces people. Dams help (water, electricity) but also change a landscape forever.

questions.question: How does ROAD BUILDING change the landscape?
questions.ruby_prompt: How does road building change the natural landscape?
options: It cuts through hills, fills valleys, drains wetlands and removes vegetation
questions.expected: It cuts through hills, fills valleys, drains wetlands and removes vegetation
questions.memo: Roads need flat surfaces. So engineers cut into hills, fill in low spots, and clear plants. This is necessary but it does change the land permanently.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa has a COAST on both the Atlantic AND Indian Ocean.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: South Africa has a coast on both the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. The west coast is the cold Atlantic; the east coast is the warm Indian Ocean. The two meet near Cape Agulhas — the southern tip of Africa.

questions.question: What is a CAPE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a cape (in geography)?
options: A piece of land that sticks out into the sea
questions.expected: A piece of land that sticks out into the sea
questions.memo: Cape Point and Cape Agulhas are famous SA capes. The Cape province got its name from these points of land sticking into the sea.

questions.question: Tell me ONE physical feature near where you live.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one physical feature near where you live — a river, hill, mountain, valley, anything.
questions.expected: The Jukskei river flows near my home
questions.memo: Good answers: a river, hill, mountain, valley, coast, koppie, beach, gorge. Any real feature of the local landscape.

questions.question: Why do most South African CITIES lie on the COAST or on RIVERS?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are most major South African cities on the coast or near rivers?
options: People settled near water — for drinking, farming, fishing and trade
questions.expected: People settled near water — for drinking, farming, fishing and trade
questions.memo: Water is life. Cape Town, Durban, East London, Port Elizabeth are coastal. Joburg is unusual — built around GOLD, not water (which is why it imports water from far away).

SS.L5.GEO.T03.title: Weather, climate and vegetation of South Africa
SS.L5.GEO.T03.description: Elements of weather; difference between weather and climate; rainfall patterns; natural vegetation including savannah grasslands.
SS.L5.GEO.T03.recovery_strategy: Weather = TODAY. Climate = the PATTERN over many years. Natural vegetation is plants that grow on their own, shaped by climate. Different climates grow different plants.

questions.question: What is the difference between WEATHER and CLIMATE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the difference between weather and climate?
options: Weather is what's happening today; climate is the pattern over many years
They mean exactly the same thing
Weather is hot; climate is cold
Climate only happens at the coast
questions.expected: Weather is what's happening today; climate is the pattern over many years
questions.memo: Weather changes day to day — rain today, sun tomorrow. Climate is the long-run pattern of a place, built up over many years.

questions.question: Which is an ELEMENT of weather?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is an element of weather?
options: Temperature, wind, cloud cover and rainfall
questions.expected: Temperature, wind, cloud cover and rainfall
questions.memo: Weather has several parts — how hot/cold (temperature), how windy, how cloudy, and how much rain. All four together describe the weather.

questions.question: What is 'PRECIPITATION'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does precipitation mean?
options: Water that falls from the sky — rain, hail or snow
questions.expected: Water that falls from the sky — rain, hail or snow
questions.memo: Precipitation = any water falling from clouds. Most of SA gets rain; high mountains get snow in winter; some places get hail with summer storms.

questions.question: What instrument measures TEMPERATURE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What instrument measures temperature?
questions.expected: A thermometer
questions.memo: Thermometers measure how hot or cold the air is — usually in degrees Celsius in South Africa.

questions.question: What instrument measures RAINFALL?
questions.ruby_prompt: What instrument measures rainfall?
questions.expected: A rain gauge
questions.memo: A rain gauge collects rain. You can read off the depth in millimetres. A simple jar with a ruler works as a homemade rain gauge.

questions.question: What does a WIND SOCK or WIND VANE show?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a wind sock or wind vane show you?
options: The direction the wind is blowing from
questions.expected: The direction the wind is blowing from
questions.memo: Wind direction matters — for weather forecasts, for pilots, for sailors. We name a wind by where it comes FROM (a 'south-east wind' blows from the south-east).

questions.question: Most of South Africa gets its rain in:
questions.ruby_prompt: Most of South Africa gets its rain in which season?
questions.expected: Summer (October to March)
questions.memo: Most of SA is a SUMMER rainfall area. Big thunderstorms come in summer afternoons. The Western Cape is the main exception — see the next question.

questions.question: Which part of South Africa gets WINTER rainfall?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which part of South Africa gets most of its rain in winter?
questions.expected: The Western Cape (around Cape Town)
questions.memo: Cape Town has a winter rainfall climate — like the Mediterranean. Hot dry summers and wet cool winters. The fynbos plants of the Cape evolved for this.

questions.question: What is 'NATURAL VEGETATION'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is natural vegetation?
options: Plants that grow on their own in an area, without being planted by humans
questions.expected: Plants that grow on their own in an area, without being planted by humans
questions.memo: Natural vegetation is what GROWS THERE BY ITSELF — shaped by climate, soil and water. Different climates = different vegetation.

questions.question: What is a 'SAVANNAH'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a savannah?
options: A warm grassland with scattered trees — like the bushveld and Kruger area
questions.expected: A warm grassland with scattered trees — like the bushveld and Kruger area
questions.memo: Savannah = grass with trees here and there. Found in warm areas with a wet summer and dry winter. Home to many of Africa's famous animals.

questions.question: Why do most savannah trees have SMALL or NEEDLE-LIKE leaves?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do many savannah trees have small or needle-like leaves?
options: Small leaves lose less water — useful in a dry climate
Small leaves are easier to draw
questions.expected: Small leaves lose less water — useful in a dry climate
questions.memo: Plants adapt to climate. Big leaves lose lots of water; small or needle leaves lose less. Acacia and karoo plants show this beautifully.

questions.question: True or false: Climate affects what kind of CLOTHES people wear.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: climate affects what clothes people wear.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. In hot climates, light and loose clothes; in cold climates, warm layers. Daily life everywhere is shaped by climate.

questions.question: Why is the Western Cape called a 'MEDITERRANEAN' climate?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is the Western Cape called a Mediterranean climate?
options: Hot dry summers and cool wet winters — same as the Mediterranean coast of Europe
questions.expected: Hot dry summers and cool wet winters — same as the Mediterranean coast of Europe
questions.memo: Same climate, half a world apart. That's why grapes, olives and wheat (Mediterranean plants) grow so well in the Cape.

questions.question: Why is GAUTENG often hot in summer with afternoon thunderstorms?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does Gauteng often have hot summers with afternoon thunderstorms?
options: The hot air rises during the day, cools and forms clouds and storms by afternoon
questions.expected: The hot air rises during the day, cools and forms clouds and storms by afternoon
questions.memo: Highveld summers = sunny mornings, building clouds by lunch, thunderstorms by 3–4pm. A real pattern. The sun's heating drives the daily cycle.

questions.question: Put these in order from WETTEST to DRIEST in South Africa.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order from wettest to driest in South Africa.
questions.expected: KwaZulu-Natal coast (very wet),Gauteng (summer rains),Karoo (dry, some rain),Northern Cape / Namib edge (very dry)
questions.memo: SA dries out as you move from east to west. The Indian Ocean side gets wet air; the Atlantic side gets dry air.

questions.question: How does CLIMATE affect what FARMERS can grow?
questions.ruby_prompt: How does climate affect what farmers can grow?
options: Different climates suit different crops — maize needs summer rain, wheat needs winter rain
questions.expected: Different climates suit different crops — maize needs summer rain, wheat needs winter rain
questions.memo: Wheat in the Western Cape (winter rain), maize on the Highveld (summer rain), sugar cane in KZN (warm and wet). The map of farming follows the climate map.

questions.question: True or false: ANIMALS in the savannah are linked to the natural vegetation.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: animals in a savannah are linked to the natural vegetation.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Zebra and wildebeest eat grass; giraffes eat tree leaves; lions eat the grass-eaters. Take away the plants — the animal world falls apart.

questions.question: Why do FARMERS WATCH the weather forecast?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do farmers watch the weather forecast carefully?
options: Weather decides when to plant, when to harvest, when to protect animals from cold or storms
Weather has no effect on farming
Only city people watch the weather
questions.expected: Weather decides when to plant, when to harvest, when to protect animals from cold or storms
questions.memo: A wrong-timed planting can lose a crop. A frost can kill lambs. Farmers and weather forecasters are old partners.

questions.question: Tell me what the WEATHER is like where you live in WINTER.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me what the weather is like where you live in winter.
questions.expected: Where I live the winters are cold and dry with frost in the mornings
questions.memo: Good answers describe real local conditions — cold, dry, frosty (Gauteng); cool and rainy (Cape Town); warm but dry (KZN coast); mild (Durban). All real.

questions.question: Which BEST describes South Africa's climate overall?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which best describes South Africa's climate overall?
options: Varied — different climates in different regions, mostly warm and dry
questions.expected: Varied — different climates in different regions, mostly warm and dry
questions.memo: SA's climate varies a lot — coastal vs inland, summer rain vs winter rain, hot Lowveld vs cool Highveld. This variety is part of what makes the country so rich.

SS.L5.GEO.T04.title: Minerals and mining in South Africa
SS.L5.GEO.T04.description: SA's main minerals (gold, platinum, diamonds, iron ore, coal); ways of mining; environmental impact; health and safety of miners.
SS.L5.GEO.T04.recovery_strategy: Minerals are non-renewable — once mined, they're gone. SA is famous for gold, platinum and diamonds. Mining brings wealth but can hurt land, air, water and miners' health.

questions.question: What is a 'MINERAL'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a mineral?
options: A natural substance found in the earth — like gold, iron or diamond
questions.expected: A natural substance found in the earth — like gold, iron or diamond
questions.memo: Minerals come from rocks in the earth. Some are very valuable (gold, platinum, diamonds); others are useful in big quantities (iron, coal).

questions.question: What does 'NON-RENEWABLE' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does non-renewable mean?
options: Once used up, it cannot grow back — it is gone forever
It is a type of plant
questions.expected: Once used up, it cannot grow back — it is gone forever
questions.memo: Minerals took millions of years to form. Once mined and used, we cannot make new ones. That's why we use them carefully.

questions.question: Which mineral is South Africa MOST famous for?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which mineral is South Africa most famous for?
questions.expected: Gold
questions.memo: South Africa was the world's biggest gold producer for many decades. Johannesburg ('eGoli — place of gold') was built on it.

questions.question: Which is ANOTHER very important South African mineral?
questions.ruby_prompt: Besides gold, which other mineral is South Africa world-famous for?
questions.expected: Platinum
questions.memo: South Africa has most of the world's platinum. Used in car parts, jewellery, electronics and medical equipment.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa mines DIAMONDS.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: South Africa mines diamonds.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Kimberley is famous for diamond mining. The Big Hole there was dug entirely by hand — one of the largest hand-dug holes in the world.

questions.question: What is COAL used for?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is coal used for?
options: To generate electricity and make steel
questions.expected: To generate electricity and make steel
questions.memo: Most of SA's electricity comes from coal-fired power stations. Coal also helps make steel. But burning coal pollutes the air, so the world is moving away from it.

questions.question: Is COAL technically a 'MINERAL'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Is coal technically a mineral?
options: No — it is formed from old plant remains, but we still mine it like a mineral
Yes, exactly the same as a mineral
questions.expected: No — it is formed from old plant remains, but we still mine it like a mineral
questions.memo: Coal formed from ancient plants buried millions of years ago. Scientists call it a fossil fuel, not a mineral — but we mine and treat it like a mineral.

questions.question: What is OPEN-PIT mining?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is open-pit mining?
options: Digging a huge hole from the surface to reach minerals near the top of the ground
questions.expected: Digging a huge hole from the surface to reach minerals near the top of the ground
questions.memo: If the mineral is near the surface, open-pit mining is cheaper and faster. The Big Hole in Kimberley and Palabora copper mine are examples.

questions.question: What is DEEP-LEVEL (shaft) mining?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is deep-level shaft mining?
options: Digging deep shafts and tunnels underground to reach minerals far below the surface
questions.expected: Digging deep shafts and tunnels underground to reach minerals far below the surface
questions.memo: South Africa has some of the deepest mines in the world — some go DOWN over 3km. Gold and platinum are mined this way.

questions.question: What is the BIG environmental problem with mining?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a big environmental problem with mining?
options: It pollutes water and air, destroys vegetation, and leaves big waste piles
questions.expected: It pollutes water and air, destroys vegetation, and leaves big waste piles
questions.memo: Mining changes land permanently. Dust gets into the air, chemicals into water, plants and animals lose habitat. Modern mining tries to limit these effects.

questions.question: What is SILICOSIS?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is silicosis — a disease miners can get?
options: A lung disease from breathing in dust over many years underground
questions.expected: A lung disease from breathing in dust over many years underground
questions.memo: Underground rock dust hurts the lungs. Many South African miners have silicosis from years working in deep mines. Mines now MUST control dust.

questions.question: Why is it HOT deep underground?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it so hot deep underground in a mine?
options: The earth gets hotter the deeper you go
questions.expected: The earth gets hotter the deeper you go
questions.memo: The deeper the mine, the hotter the rocks. SA's deep gold mines reach over 50°C without cooling. Big fans and ice are used to make it survivable.

questions.question: Which is a RULE that protects miners?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a safety rule that protects miners?
options: Wearing helmets, masks and boots; following safety procedures; regular inspections
questions.expected: Wearing helmets, masks and boots; following safety procedures; regular inspections
questions.memo: Mining is dangerous. Safety equipment, training, ventilation and inspections save lives. Workers also have unions to push for better conditions.

questions.question: Why does South Africa MINE in the first place?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does South Africa mine so much?
options: The country has rich mineral deposits, and mining earns big income and many jobs
questions.expected: The country has rich mineral deposits, and mining earns big income and many jobs
questions.memo: Mining built modern SA. It earns export money, employs hundreds of thousands of people, and supports many other industries.

questions.question: Put these in order — what happens to a piece of GOLD from underground to a shop.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order — what happens to gold from underground to a jewellery shop.
options: Miners dig up the gold-bearing rock deep underground
Rock is brought to the surface and crushed
Gold is separated from the rock and melted into bars
Bars are sold and made into jewellery or kept as wealth
questions.expected: Miners dig up the gold-bearing rock deep underground,Rock is brought to the surface and crushed,Gold is separated from the rock and melted into bars,Bars are sold and made into jewellery or kept as wealth
questions.memo: Mine → crush → separate → melt → trade. A long, expensive process. That's part of why gold is so valuable.

questions.question: What is IRON ORE used for?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is iron ore used for?
options: Making steel — used in buildings, cars, ships, machines
questions.expected: Making steel — used in buildings, cars, ships, machines
questions.memo: Iron ore is the start of most steel. Steel is in almost everything modern — bridges, cars, fridges, knives. SA has big iron ore mines like Sishen.

questions.question: True or false: All of South Africa's MINERAL wealth will last forever.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: South Africa's mineral wealth will last forever.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: False. Mines run out. As old mines close, communities must find new work. Mining areas need to plan for life AFTER mining.

questions.question: Lerato's father works in a deep gold mine. What is one DANGER he faces?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato's father works in a deep gold mine. What's one danger he faces?
options: Rock falls, heat, dust, and equipment accidents
questions.expected: Rock falls, heat, dust, and equipment accidents
questions.memo: Deep mining is one of the hardest jobs in the world. Strict safety procedures save lives. Many miners support whole families with their work.

questions.question: Tell me ONE everyday item that uses a MINERAL.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one everyday item that uses a mineral.
questions.expected: My cell phone uses gold and other metals
questions.memo: Good answers: cell phone (gold, copper, rare metals), car (iron/steel, aluminium, platinum), jewellery, batteries, electric wires, money (copper coins). All real.

questions.question: What is the BIGGEST lesson about mining?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the biggest lesson about mining and the country?
options: Mining gives wealth and jobs but must balance environment, safety and the future
Mining is purely good with no problems
Mining is purely bad with no benefits
questions.expected: Mining gives wealth and jobs but must balance environment, safety and the future
questions.memo: Mining is both/and — wealth AND damage. The challenge is to mine in a way that's fair to workers, kind to the environment, and plans for the future.

SS.L6.HIS.T01.title: An African kingdom long ago: Mapungubwe
SS.L6.HIS.T01.description: Mapungubwe (1220–1300) — first state in Southern Africa; trade across the Indian Ocean; gold objects; Great Zimbabwe; Marco Polo's travels.
SS.L6.HIS.T01.recovery_strategy: Mapungubwe was a kingdom in the Limpopo Valley about 800 years ago — the first state in Southern Africa. It traded across the Indian Ocean. The famous gold rhino was a royal symbol.

questions.question: Where was MAPUNGUBWE?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where was Mapungubwe?
options: In the Limpopo Valley, in the north of South Africa
questions.expected: In the Limpopo Valley, in the north of South Africa
questions.memo: Mapungubwe is at the meeting point of South Africa, Botswana and Zimbabwe. Its hill stands above the surrounding flat land.

questions.question: Roughly WHEN did Mapungubwe rise to power?
questions.ruby_prompt: Roughly when did Mapungubwe rise to power?
questions.expected: About 800 years ago (1220–1300)
questions.memo: Mapungubwe was at its height between 1220 and 1300 AD — about 800 years ago, long before any Europeans arrived in Southern Africa.

questions.question: Why is Mapungubwe IMPORTANT in South African history?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is Mapungubwe so important in South African history?
options: It was the FIRST state (kingdom) in Southern Africa
questions.expected: It was the FIRST state (kingdom) in Southern Africa
questions.memo: Before Mapungubwe, Southern African groups were chiefdoms. Mapungubwe was bigger, more organised — a true state with classes, a king, and international trade.

questions.question: What was the famous GOLDEN object found at Mapungubwe?
questions.ruby_prompt: What famous golden object was found at Mapungubwe?
questions.expected: A small gold rhinoceros (royal symbol)
questions.memo: The gold rhino is one of South Africa's greatest historical treasures — a symbol of royal power, made by skilled craftsmen 800 years ago.

questions.question: What did Mapungubwe TRADE across the Indian Ocean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What did Mapungubwe trade across the Indian Ocean?
options: Gold, ivory and animal skins — for glass beads, cloth and ceramics
questions.expected: Gold, ivory and animal skins — for glass beads, cloth and ceramics
questions.memo: Mapungubwe was connected to a huge trading world — its goods reached India, Persia and China. Glass beads from far away have been found at the site.

questions.question: What was MAPUNGUBWE HILL used for?
questions.ruby_prompt: What was Mapungubwe Hill used for?
options: The king and royal family lived on top, while others lived below — a sign of class division
questions.expected: The king and royal family lived on top, while others lived below — a sign of class division
questions.memo: Living high meant being above — physically and socially. The hill itself was a symbol of royal power and a real change in how Southern African society was organised.

questions.question: What is the 'ORDER OF MAPUNGUBWE'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Order of Mapungubwe?
options: South Africa's highest honour, given for exceptional achievement and service
questions.expected: South Africa's highest honour, given for exceptional achievement and service
questions.memo: South Africa named its highest honour after Mapungubwe — recognising African heritage and the importance of this early kingdom.

questions.question: What is GREAT ZIMBABWE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is Great Zimbabwe?
options: A large stone-walled city that succeeded Mapungubwe as a centre of trade
questions.expected: A large stone-walled city that succeeded Mapungubwe as a centre of trade
questions.memo: Great Zimbabwe — in modern Zimbabwe — rose AFTER Mapungubwe and was even bigger. Its massive stone walls were built without mortar. The country Zimbabwe is named after it.

questions.question: Who was MARCO POLO?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Marco Polo?
options: A European traveller from Italy who journeyed to Asia in the 1200s
questions.expected: A European traveller from Italy who journeyed to Asia in the 1200s
questions.memo: Marco Polo travelled overland from Italy to China at the same time as Mapungubwe was rising. He wrote a book about Asia that fascinated Europeans for centuries.

questions.question: Why is Mapungubwe a WORLD HERITAGE SITE?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is Mapungubwe a World Heritage Site?
options: It is of huge importance to global history — recognised by UNESCO
It is the biggest country in Africa
questions.expected: It is of huge importance to global history — recognised by UNESCO
questions.memo: UNESCO World Heritage means an outstanding place that belongs to all of humanity. Mapungubwe earned this recognition in 2003.

questions.question: Put these in chronological order.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in chronological order, oldest first.
questions.expected: First Bantu-speaking farmers (about 1700 years ago),Settlements at K2 and Schroda,Mapungubwe at its height (1220–1300),Great Zimbabwe at its height (later)
questions.memo: Each builds on the one before. Farmers settle → small settlements grow → first kingdom (Mapungubwe) → even bigger one (Great Zimbabwe).

questions.question: True or false: Mapungubwe was connected to the rest of the WORLD through trade.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Mapungubwe was connected to the rest of the world through trade.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Trading networks reached from the Limpopo Valley to East Africa and onwards to India and China — globalisation 800 years ago.

questions.question: What kind of GOODS came IN to Mapungubwe from trade?
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of goods came in to Mapungubwe from trade?
options: Glass beads, cloth and ceramics from across the Indian Ocean
questions.expected: Glass beads, cloth and ceramics from across the Indian Ocean
questions.memo: Beautiful glass beads, cloth and pottery were the IMPORTS. Mapungubwe people valued these and used them as signs of wealth.

questions.question: How did people TRAVEL between Mapungubwe and the East Coast?
questions.ruby_prompt: How did traders travel between Mapungubwe and the East Coast?
options: On foot, along established trading routes — a journey of weeks
questions.expected: On foot, along established trading routes — a journey of weeks
questions.memo: All overland travel was on foot. Traders carried goods, knew the routes, faced wild animals and weather. A real adventure, every trip.

questions.question: What does the GOLD RHINO show us about Mapungubwe?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the gold rhino tell us about Mapungubwe society?
options: They had skilled craftspeople, royal power, wealth, and African art of high quality
questions.expected: They had skilled craftspeople, royal power, wealth, and African art of high quality
questions.memo: A small object tells a big story — skilled workers, kings worth honouring, wealth, and artistry. Mapungubwe wasn't simple — it was a sophisticated society.

questions.question: Why does Mapungubwe matter for SOUTH AFRICAN IDENTITY today?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is Mapungubwe important for South African identity today?
options: It proves Africa had advanced kingdoms and global trade long before Europeans arrived
Because it is on a coin
Because it is in a song
questions.expected: It proves Africa had advanced kingdoms and global trade long before Europeans arrived
questions.memo: For a long time history books said African civilisations only began with Europeans. Mapungubwe is direct evidence against that — and now part of how SA understands itself.

questions.question: True or false: Mapungubwe had DISTINCT SOCIAL CLASSES (king, nobles, ordinary people).
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Mapungubwe had distinct social classes — king, nobles, ordinary people.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. A change from earlier chiefdoms where everyone was much more equal. Mapungubwe's royal family lived on top of the hill — others below.

questions.question: What happened to MAPUNGUBWE around 1300?
questions.ruby_prompt: What happened to Mapungubwe around the year 1300?
options: It declined as people moved away — possibly due to drought and shifting trade
questions.expected: It declined as people moved away — possibly due to drought and shifting trade
questions.memo: All kingdoms rise and fall. Mapungubwe declined; people drifted away; eventually Great Zimbabwe to the north took over the trading role.

questions.question: Tell me ONE thing that surprises or impresses you about Mapungubwe.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing about Mapungubwe that surprises or impresses you.
questions.expected: I'm impressed that they traded all the way to China 800 years ago
questions.memo: Good answers: international trade, the gold rhino, the stone palace, social classes, that it existed before Europeans, that it's a World Heritage Site. All real.

questions.question: Which BEST describes Mapungubwe?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which best describes Mapungubwe?
options: A sophisticated African kingdom of trade, art and royal power that existed 800 years ago
questions.expected: A sophisticated African kingdom of trade, art and royal power that existed 800 years ago
questions.memo: Sophisticated, connected, organised, artistic — and AFRICAN. That's Mapungubwe. A reminder that African history is rich and ancient.

SS.L6.HIS.T02.title: Explorers from Europe find Southern Africa
SS.L6.HIS.T02.description: The European Renaissance; new inventions; reasons for exploration; Dias and Da Gama; the VOC.
SS.L6.HIS.T02.recovery_strategy: The Renaissance gave Europe new ideas and tools (compass, caravel). Europeans wanted a sea route to ASIA for trade. On the way they sailed past Southern Africa — but didn't yet settle.

questions.question: What was the RENAISSANCE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What was the Renaissance?
options: A 'rebirth' of new ideas, art and learning in Europe (15th–16th centuries)
questions.expected: A 'rebirth' of new ideas, art and learning in Europe (15th–16th centuries)
questions.memo: Renaissance means 'rebirth' in French. After centuries of slower growth, Europe burst into a period of art, science, exploration and big new ideas.

questions.question: Who was LEONARDO DA VINCI?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Leonardo da Vinci?
options: An Italian Renaissance artist, scientist and inventor
questions.expected: An Italian Renaissance artist, scientist and inventor
questions.memo: Leonardo painted the Mona Lisa, designed flying machines (centuries before planes), and studied anatomy. A symbol of the Renaissance mind.

questions.question: Who was GALILEO?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Galileo?
options: An Italian scientist who used a telescope and showed the earth moves around the sun
questions.expected: An Italian scientist who used a telescope and showed the earth moves around the sun
questions.memo: Galileo improved the telescope and proved old ideas wrong with his observations of the stars. He got into trouble with the Church for his discoveries.

questions.question: What did the MAGNETIC COMPASS allow sailors to do?
questions.ruby_prompt: What did the magnetic compass allow sailors to do?
options: Know which direction they were heading, even out of sight of land
questions.expected: Know which direction they were heading, even out of sight of land
questions.memo: Before the compass, sailors needed to stay near land. The compass let them cross open ocean confidently — a game-changer for exploration.

questions.question: What is GUNPOWDER?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is gunpowder?
options: A powder that explodes — used in guns and cannons
questions.expected: A powder that explodes — used in guns and cannons
questions.memo: Originally invented in China. Once in Europe it changed warfare — castles and armour couldn't stop cannons. It also helped Europeans dominate other places militarily.

questions.question: What is a CARAVEL?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a caravel?
options: A small sailing ship that could travel far against the wind
questions.expected: A small sailing ship that could travel far against the wind
questions.memo: Caravels could tack — sail at angles to the wind, even almost into it. This let them explore against currents and return home safely.

questions.question: Why did EUROPEANS want a sea route to ASIA?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why did Europeans want a sea route to Asia?
options: To trade for spices, silk and other valuable goods directly
questions.expected: To trade for spices, silk and other valuable goods directly
questions.memo: Asian spices (pepper, cloves, nutmeg) and silks were extremely valuable in Europe. Overland routes were long and other people controlled them. A sea route = more profit.

questions.question: Who was BARTOLOMEU DIAS?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Bartolomeu Dias?
options: A Portuguese explorer who first rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488
questions.expected: A Portuguese explorer who first rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488
questions.memo: In 1488 Dias became the first European to sail around the bottom of Africa. A storm pushed him round — and proved the sea route to India was possible.

questions.question: Where did Dias and his crew MEET the Khoikhoi?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where did Dias and his crew meet the Khoikhoi?
options: Mossel Bay (on the South African coast) in 1488
questions.expected: Mossel Bay (on the South African coast) in 1488
questions.memo: Mossel Bay is where European and Southern African worlds first met face to face. The Khoikhoi already lived there for many generations.

questions.question: Who was VASCO DA GAMA?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Vasco da Gama?
options: A Portuguese explorer who sailed from Europe to India around Africa (1497–98)
questions.expected: A Portuguese explorer who sailed from Europe to India around Africa (1497–98)
questions.memo: Da Gama completed what Dias began — actually reaching India by sea. His voyage opened a new era of European trade and colonisation.

questions.question: What was the VOC?
questions.ruby_prompt: What was the VOC?
options: The Dutch East India Company — a powerful trading company
questions.expected: The Dutch East India Company — a powerful trading company
questions.memo: The VOC (Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie) controlled Dutch trade with Asia. It later set up the Cape supply station in 1652 — the start of European settlement here.

questions.question: What was life like for a SAILOR on a VOC ship?
questions.ruby_prompt: What was life like for a sailor on a VOC ship?
options: Hard, dangerous, with poor food, storms, illness, and tight discipline
questions.expected: Hard, dangerous, with poor food, storms, illness, and tight discipline
questions.memo: Sailors faced disease (scurvy from lack of vitamin C), storms, rats, terrible food, strict captains, and months at sea. Many died on these voyages.

questions.question: Put these in chronological order — European exploration.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in chronological order — moments in European exploration.
options: The Renaissance brings new ideas and inventions
Dias rounds the southern tip of Africa (1488)
The Dutch (VOC) settle at the Cape (1652)
questions.expected: The Renaissance brings new ideas and inventions,Dias rounds the southern tip of Africa (1488),Da Gama reaches India (1498),The Dutch (VOC) settle at the Cape (1652)
questions.memo: Ideas → exploration → reaching the destination → settling along the route. Each step built on the previous.

questions.question: True or false: Before 1488, Europeans knew very LITTLE about Southern Africa.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: before 1488, Europeans knew very little about Southern Africa.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Europeans had heard rumours of African gold and trade routes but had never sailed past the equator. Africa south of the Sahara was a mystery to them.

questions.question: Why did 'spreading the CHRISTIAN religion' motivate some explorers?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why did spreading the Christian religion motivate some European explorers?
options: They believed it was their religious duty to spread their beliefs to others
questions.expected: They believed it was their religious duty to spread their beliefs to others
questions.memo: Many explorers genuinely believed they were doing God's work by converting others — alongside (sometimes in tension with) the goal of trade and profit.

questions.question: What did the EXPLORERS' arrival mean for AFRICAN people in the long run?
questions.ruby_prompt: What did the arrival of European explorers eventually mean for African people?
options: The beginning of European trade — and later colonisation, conflict and loss of land
African life stayed exactly the same
questions.expected: The beginning of European trade — and later colonisation, conflict and loss of land
questions.memo: Exploration led to settlement, then colonisation, then loss of land and dignity for many African peoples. This is the story that runs through Grades 7-9 history.

questions.question: Where did Europeans LEARN ideas from (besides their own)?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where did Europeans learn ideas from during the Renaissance — besides Europe?
options: From Arab, Chinese and African knowledge as well
questions.expected: From Arab, Chinese and African knowledge as well
questions.memo: Many Renaissance ideas (gunpowder from China, navigation from Arab traders, mathematics from many places) came from outside Europe. Knowledge flows around the world.

questions.question: True or false: The Khoikhoi were the FIRST people in Southern Africa to meet Europeans.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the Khoikhoi were the first people in Southern Africa to meet Europeans.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. As herders along the coast, the Khoikhoi were the first to encounter Portuguese, then Dutch, then British ships. Often the encounters were tense.

questions.question: Tell me ONE invention that helped European exploration.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one invention that helped European exploration.
questions.expected: The compass helped sailors know which direction they were heading
questions.memo: Good answers: compass, caravel ship, gunpowder, printing press (for spreading maps), astrolabe for navigation. All real.

questions.question: Which BEST describes the European arrival in Southern Africa?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which best describes the European arrival in Southern Africa?
options: The start of contact that would eventually transform — and badly harm — many African societies
questions.expected: The start of contact that would eventually transform — and badly harm — many African societies
questions.memo: First contact looked small. But it set in motion centuries of trade, settlement, colonisation, slavery and apartheid. We're still living with the consequences.

SS.L6.HIS.T03.title: Democracy and citizenship in South Africa
SS.L6.HIS.T03.description: South Africa's first democratic election in 1994; the Constitution; Parliament; rights and responsibilities; the Constitutional Court; children's rights; national symbols.
SS.L6.HIS.T03.recovery_strategy: Democracy means the people choose the government. South Africa became a democracy in 1994 after the struggle against apartheid. The Constitution is the highest law and protects every person's rights.

questions.question: In what year did South Africa hold its first DEMOCRATIC election?
questions.ruby_prompt: In what year did South Africa hold its first democratic election — the one where everyone could vote?
questions.memo: 27 April 1994 — the first time all South Africans, regardless of race, could vote. Nelson Mandela became the country's first democratically elected president.

questions.question: What does 'DEMOCRACY' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does democracy mean?
options: A system where the people choose their government by voting
questions.expected: A system where the people choose their government by voting
questions.memo: Democracy comes from Greek — 'demos' (people) + 'kratos' (power). The PEOPLE have the power to choose leaders, change laws and hold government accountable.

questions.question: What is APARTHEID?
questions.ruby_prompt: What was apartheid?
options: A South African system that unfairly separated people by race and denied rights to non-white people
questions.expected: A South African system that unfairly separated people by race and denied rights to non-white people
questions.memo: Apartheid (Afrikaans for 'separateness') was the law in SA from 1948 to 1994. It treated people differently based on skin colour. The fight to end it shaped modern SA.

questions.question: Who became South Africa's FIRST democratically elected president?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who became South Africa's first democratically elected president?
questions.expected: Nelson Mandela
questions.memo: After 27 years in prison, Mandela led the negotiations that ended apartheid, then won the 1994 election. He served one term and stepped down.

questions.question: What is the CONSTITUTION?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the South African Constitution?
options: The highest law of the country — sets out rights and how government works
questions.expected: The highest law of the country — sets out rights and how government works
questions.memo: Our Constitution (adopted in 1996) is the rulebook. No law can be against it. It protects every person's rights and tells government what it can and can't do.

questions.question: What is PARLIAMENT?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is Parliament?
options: The body of elected representatives who make laws for the country
questions.expected: The body of elected representatives who make laws for the country
questions.memo: Parliament is where the people we elect meet to discuss and pass laws. South Africa's Parliament is in Cape Town.

questions.question: True or false: In a democracy, every adult citizen has ONE VOTE.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: in a democracy, every adult citizen has one vote.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. 'One person, one vote' — the heart of democracy. A taxi driver's vote counts the same as a millionaire's vote.

questions.question: What is the CONSTITUTIONAL COURT?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Constitutional Court?
options: The highest court — decides if laws and actions follow the Constitution
questions.expected: The highest court — decides if laws and actions follow the Constitution
questions.memo: The Concourt protects the Constitution. If a law violates rights, it can be struck down — even if Parliament passed it. A powerful safeguard for democracy.

questions.question: Who was PIUS LANGA?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Pius Langa?
options: Chief Justice of South Africa and head of the Constitutional Court (2005–2009)
questions.expected: Chief Justice of South Africa and head of the Constitutional Court (2005–2009)
questions.memo: Pius Langa rose from humble origins to become Chief Justice. He played a key role in shaping a fair, equal South African legal system. A democracy hero.

questions.question: Who was FATIMA MEER?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Fatima Meer?
options: An anti-apartheid activist, writer and friend of Mandela who helped build democracy
questions.expected: An anti-apartheid activist, writer and friend of Mandela who helped build democracy
questions.memo: Fatima Meer fought apartheid for decades, faced banning orders, wrote Mandela's first authorised biography. Many ordinary heroes built South African democracy — she was one.

questions.question: Which is a RIGHT of every South African citizen?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a right of every South African citizen?
options: The right to life, dignity, equality, freedom of speech and a fair trial
The right to break any law
The right to take other people's things
questions.expected: The right to life, dignity, equality, freedom of speech and a fair trial
questions.memo: The Bill of Rights (Chapter 2 of the Constitution) protects these. Every person — born here or not — has these rights.

questions.question: Which is a RESPONSIBILITY of a good citizen?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a responsibility of a good citizen?
options: Obeying laws, paying taxes, voting, respecting others' rights
questions.expected: Obeying laws, paying taxes, voting, respecting others' rights
questions.memo: Rights and responsibilities go together. We get the protections — and we owe the country basic good citizenship in return.

questions.question: What is the CHILDREN'S CHARTER of South Africa?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Children's Charter of South Africa?
options: A document setting out the rights and responsibilities of children in SA
questions.expected: A document setting out the rights and responsibilities of children in SA
questions.memo: Children have specific rights — to education, to be heard, to be safe, to identity. The Children's Charter expresses these and is part of the broader Constitution.

questions.question: Which is a NATIONAL SYMBOL of South Africa?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a national symbol of South Africa?
options: The Coat of Arms, the national flag, and the national anthem
questions.expected: The Coat of Arms, the national flag, and the national anthem
questions.memo: These symbols represent the country in official settings and at international events. They were chosen after 1994 to reflect the new democratic SA.

questions.question: What is in the centre of South Africa's NATIONAL FLAG?
questions.ruby_prompt: What shape is in the centre of South Africa's national flag?
options: A horizontal Y-shape — symbolising the joining of different paths into one
questions.expected: A horizontal Y-shape — symbolising the joining of different paths into one
questions.memo: The Y represents many separate paths coming together — the convergence of different histories into one shared future. Adopted in 1994.

questions.question: Put these in chronological order — South African democracy.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in chronological order — moments in the journey to democracy.
options: Apartheid laws make racial segregation official (1948)
questions.expected: Apartheid laws make racial segregation official (1948),Mandela imprisoned for fighting apartheid (1962),Mandela released from prison (1990),First democratic election (1994)
questions.memo: 1948 → 1962 → 1990 → 1994. A 46-year journey. Many people fought, many died, many sacrificed everything to win these freedoms.

questions.question: Why is it important to VOTE?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it important for citizens to vote?
options: It is how citizens choose their leaders and shape the country — and millions died for this right
questions.expected: It is how citizens choose their leaders and shape the country — and millions died for this right
questions.memo: Not voting means giving up your voice. For South Africans, voting also honours every person who fought for this right. Every election matters.

questions.question: True or false: All people are EQUAL under the law in South Africa.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: all people are equal under the law in South Africa.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True — this is part of the Constitution. Wealth, race, religion or background must not affect how the law treats you. In practice we're still working on making this fully real.

questions.question: Tell me ONE thing you would do as a good CITIZEN of South Africa.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing you can do as a good citizen of South Africa.
questions.expected: I can help keep my community clean by picking up litter
questions.memo: Good answers: be kind to neighbours, obey rules, help others, respect different cultures, look after the environment, learn about the country, plan to vote at 18.

questions.question: Why is SOUTH AFRICAN democracy SPECIAL in world history?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is South African democracy considered special in world history?
options: A racially divided country chose negotiation and reconciliation instead of civil war
questions.expected: A racially divided country chose negotiation and reconciliation instead of civil war
questions.memo: Many feared SA would fall into civil war. Instead, leaders on all sides chose to TALK. Mandela's choice of forgiveness over revenge is a model studied worldwide.

SS.L6.HIS.T04.title: Medicine through time
SS.L6.HIS.T04.description: Indigenous healing in SA; Western scientific discoveries — vaccination (Jenner), germs (Pasteur), TB (Koch), penicillin (Fleming); first heart transplant (Barnard).
SS.L6.HIS.T04.recovery_strategy: Two ways of healing: indigenous (treats whole person, uses plants and beliefs) and Western (treats the body using science). Both have helped people. Today they often work together.

questions.question: What is 'INDIGENOUS HEALING'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is indigenous healing?
options: Traditional healing methods built up by local people over many generations
questions.expected: Traditional healing methods built up by local people over many generations
questions.memo: Indigenous healing has been practised in Southern Africa for thousands of years — using local plants, knowledge of the body and spiritual practices.

questions.question: Who is a SANGOMA or NYANGA?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who is a sangoma or nyanga in South Africa?
options: A traditional healer trained to use plants, knowledge and spiritual practices to help people
questions.expected: A traditional healer trained to use plants, knowledge and spiritual practices to help people
questions.memo: Sangomas and nyangas are recognised in South Africa. Many people use both traditional healers AND clinics. Each can help with different things.

questions.question: What does it mean to treat someone 'HOLISTICALLY'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does it mean to treat someone holistically?
options: Caring for the WHOLE person — body, mind and spirit together
questions.expected: Caring for the WHOLE person — body, mind and spirit together
questions.memo: Holistic = the whole person. Indigenous healers have always done this. Today, modern Western medicine is also moving towards a more holistic approach.

questions.question: True or false: Many medicines today come from PLANTS used by traditional healers.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: many modern medicines come from plants that traditional healers have used for centuries.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Aspirin came from willow bark; many cancer drugs came from plants in Africa, Asia and South America. Indigenous knowledge has helped modern medicine a lot.

questions.question: Who was EDWARD JENNER?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Edward Jenner?
options: A British doctor who created the first vaccine — against smallpox
questions.expected: A British doctor who created the first vaccine — against smallpox
questions.memo: In 1796 Jenner noticed milkmaids who had cowpox didn't get smallpox. He used cowpox material to protect people from the killer smallpox disease. The first vaccine.

questions.question: What is a VACCINATION?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a vaccination?
options: A small dose of weakened or dead germs that teaches the body to fight that disease
A general medicine for any disease
questions.expected: A small dose of weakened or dead germs that teaches the body to fight that disease
questions.memo: Vaccines train your immune system without making you sick. Diseases that used to kill millions (smallpox, polio, measles) are now rare because of vaccines.

questions.question: Who was LOUIS PASTEUR?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Louis Pasteur?
options: A French scientist who proved that germs cause many diseases
questions.expected: A French scientist who proved that germs cause many diseases
questions.memo: Pasteur showed that invisible 'germs' (bacteria) cause infection. Once doctors knew this, they could sterilise tools and save many lives. He also invented pasteurisation.

questions.question: Who discovered the GERM that causes TB?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who discovered the germ (bacterium) that causes tuberculosis (TB)?
questions.expected: Robert Koch, a German doctor
questions.memo: In 1882 Koch identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the cause of TB. This made TB much easier to fight. TB is still a serious disease in SA today.

questions.question: Who discovered PENICILLIN — the first antibiotic?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who discovered penicillin — the first antibiotic?
questions.expected: Alexander Fleming, a Scottish doctor (1928)
questions.memo: Fleming noticed a mould (Penicillium) killing bacteria on his lab dish. From that accidental observation came antibiotics — one of the great gifts of modern medicine.

questions.question: What is an ANTIBIOTIC?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is an antibiotic?
options: A medicine that kills bacteria and treats infections
questions.expected: A medicine that kills bacteria and treats infections
questions.memo: Antibiotics changed medicine. Wounds that used to kill (just a cut!) became treatable. We must use them carefully though — overuse makes them stop working.

questions.question: Who performed the WORLD'S FIRST heart transplant?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who performed the world's first heart transplant?
options: Christiaan Barnard, in Cape Town, South Africa in 1967
questions.expected: Christiaan Barnard, in Cape Town, South Africa in 1967
questions.memo: December 3, 1967 — at Groote Schuur Hospital, Barnard transplanted a heart from a young car-accident victim into Louis Washkansky. The first time it had ever been done.

questions.question: What is ANAESTHESIA?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is anaesthesia?
options: A medicine that makes a patient feel no pain during surgery
questions.expected: A medicine that makes a patient feel no pain during surgery
questions.memo: Before anaesthesia, surgery was a brutal, often deadly experience. Patients had to be awake. Anaesthesia made modern surgery possible.

questions.question: What did X-RAYS allow doctors to do?
questions.ruby_prompt: What did X-rays allow doctors to do for the first time?
options: See inside the body — bones, lungs — without cutting it open
questions.expected: See inside the body — bones, lungs — without cutting it open
questions.memo: Discovered in 1895. Suddenly doctors could see a broken bone before they operated, see TB in the lungs, see pieces of metal inside a wounded soldier. A revolution.

questions.question: What is a 'BLOOD TRANSFUSION'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a blood transfusion?
options: Giving a patient blood from another person to replace what they have lost
questions.expected: Giving a patient blood from another person to replace what they have lost
questions.memo: Blood transfusion saves people who lose blood in accidents or surgery. Once we learned about blood types (1900s), transfusions became safe and routine.

questions.question: Put these in chronological order — discoveries in medicine.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in chronological order — discoveries in medicine.
questions.expected: Jenner: first vaccine against smallpox (1796),Pasteur: germs cause disease (1860s),Fleming: discovers penicillin (1928),Barnard: first heart transplant (1967)
questions.memo: Vaccine → germ theory → antibiotic → transplant. Each step depended on the discoveries before. Modern medicine is built layer by layer.

questions.question: True or false: Today, indigenous healing and Western medicine can WORK TOGETHER.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: today, indigenous healing and Western medicine can work together for patients.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Many South African doctors and traditional healers respect each other. Patients often use both — and modern medical research often studies traditional plants.

questions.question: Why was Pasteur's GERM theory such a big deal?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why was Pasteur's germ theory of disease such a huge step forward?
options: Once we knew germs cause disease, we could fight them — clean wounds, sterilise tools, develop antibiotics
It led to no other discoveries
questions.expected: Once we knew germs cause disease, we could fight them — clean wounds, sterilise tools, develop antibiotics
questions.memo: Before germ theory, doctors didn't wash hands between patients — they spread infection without knowing. Once they knew, they could stop. Millions of lives saved.

questions.question: Why is it important to PROTECT INDIGENOUS healing knowledge?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it important to protect indigenous healing knowledge?
options: It carries thousands of years of plant and healing wisdom that we might lose forever
questions.expected: It carries thousands of years of plant and healing wisdom that we might lose forever
questions.memo: If healers stop teaching their knowledge, it disappears. We may lose plant medicines that modern science hasn't even discovered yet. A real loss.

questions.question: Tell me ONE way medicine has helped someone in YOUR family.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one way medicine has helped someone in your family.
questions.expected: Antibiotics helped my sister recover from a chest infection
questions.memo: Good answers: vaccines (childhood shots), antibiotics, pain relief, surgery, dental care, eye glasses, traditional remedies for colds. All count.

questions.question: What is the BIG LESSON of 'Medicine through time'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the big lesson from this topic on medicine through time?
options: Both indigenous and Western traditions have helped humans heal — and they have more to learn from each other
questions.expected: Both indigenous and Western traditions have helped humans heal — and they have more to learn from each other
questions.memo: Neither tradition has all the answers. Mutual respect, shared learning, and good science can serve patients better than either alone. That's the modern direction.

SS.L6.GEO.T02.title: Trade (focus: South Africa and the world)
SS.L6.GEO.T02.description: Why people trade; exports and imports; raw materials vs manufactured goods; fair trade vs unfair trade.
SS.L6.GEO.T02.recovery_strategy: Trade = swapping or selling. EXPORTS go OUT of a country; IMPORTS come IN. Raw materials (cocoa beans) become more valuable when manufactured (chocolate). Fair trade = workers paid fairly.

questions.question: What is TRADE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does trade mean?
options: Exchanging goods or services — usually for money or other goods
questions.expected: Exchanging goods or services — usually for money or other goods
questions.memo: Trade can be a swap (you give me a pencil, I give you an apple) or buying with money. The basic idea is the same: exchange.

questions.question: What does 'EXPORT' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does export mean?
options: Goods that are sold OUT of a country to other countries
questions.expected: Goods that are sold OUT of a country to other countries
questions.memo: Export = exit. South African oranges sold in Europe are EXPORTS. Earning money from exports is how countries grow.

questions.question: What does 'IMPORT' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does import mean?
options: Goods that come INTO a country from other countries
questions.expected: Goods that come INTO a country from other countries
questions.memo: Import = in. Cars made in Germany sold in SA are IMPORTS. Most countries import some things they can't make well themselves.

questions.question: What is a RAW MATERIAL?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a raw material?
options: A natural product before it has been processed (e.g. wheat, gold ore, cocoa beans)
questions.expected: A natural product before it has been processed (e.g. wheat, gold ore, cocoa beans)
questions.memo: Raw materials come from farms, mines or forests. They are the START of most products — but they aren't yet usable in their final form.

questions.question: What is a MANUFACTURED good?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a manufactured good?
options: A finished product that has been made from raw materials (e.g. chocolate, jewellery, cars)
questions.expected: A finished product that has been made from raw materials (e.g. chocolate, jewellery, cars)
questions.memo: Manufactured = made in a factory. Cocoa beans → chocolate. Iron ore → steel → car. Manufacturing adds value — and earns more money.

questions.question: Put these in order — COCOA to CHOCOLATE.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order — from cocoa to chocolate.
options: Cocoa farmer grows and harvests cocoa beans
Cocoa beans are sold and shipped to factories
Factory roasts and processes beans into chocolate
Chocolate is sold in shops as a finished product
questions.expected: Cocoa farmer grows and harvests cocoa beans,Cocoa beans are sold and shipped to factories,Factory roasts and processes beans into chocolate,Chocolate is sold in shops as a finished product
questions.memo: Each step adds VALUE. The farmer earns little; the chocolate company earns most. This is true for many raw-material chains.

questions.question: Put these in order — GOLD to JEWELLERY.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order — from gold ore underground to jewellery in a shop.
options: Miners dig gold-bearing rock from underground
Gold is separated and refined into pure gold bars
Goldsmiths and factories shape gold into jewellery
questions.expected: Miners dig gold-bearing rock from underground,Gold is separated and refined into pure gold bars,Goldsmiths and factories shape gold into jewellery,Jewellery is sold in shops
questions.memo: Same pattern as cocoa: dig the raw material → refine → manufacture → sell. The miner does the hardest work but earns least.

questions.question: Which is a major South African EXPORT?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a major South African export?
questions.expected: Gold, platinum, coal, fruit, wine
questions.memo: SA exports minerals (gold, platinum, coal), fruit (apples, citrus, grapes) and wine. Earnings from these help pay for what we import.

questions.question: Which is something SOUTH AFRICA might IMPORT?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is something South Africa might import?
options: Petrol, cell phones, machines, certain medicines
questions.expected: Petrol, cell phones, machines, certain medicines
questions.memo: SA imports what it doesn't make enough of — fuel, advanced electronics, machinery. We pay for these with the export earnings.

questions.question: What is 'UNFAIR TRADE'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is unfair trade?
options: When workers are paid very little for hard work, while companies make big profits
questions.expected: When workers are paid very little for hard work, while companies make big profits
questions.memo: Unfair trade exploits workers — long hours, dangerous conditions, very low pay. The cocoa farmer might earn cents while the chocolate company earns millions.

questions.question: What is FAIR TRADE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is fair trade?
options: Trade where farmers and workers get a fair price and safe conditions
questions.expected: Trade where farmers and workers get a fair price and safe conditions
questions.memo: Fair trade pays farmers and workers properly. You sometimes pay slightly more for a fair-trade chocolate bar — but the farmer earns better.

questions.question: Why do COUNTRIES trade with each other?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do countries trade with each other?
options: No country has everything — trading lets each country focus on what it's good at
questions.expected: No country has everything — trading lets each country focus on what it's good at
questions.memo: SA has gold; Brazil has coffee; Switzerland has chocolate machines. Trade lets each country specialise — everyone gains.

questions.question: True or false: SERVICES (not just goods) can also be TRADED.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: services can also be traded between countries — not just goods.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Tourism, banking, software development, insurance — all are services. A foreign tourist visiting Cape Town is buying South African services.

questions.question: Why does a CHOCOLATE BAR cost so much MORE than the cocoa beans inside?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does a chocolate bar in a shop cost so much more than the cocoa beans inside?
options: Factory processing, packaging, transport, shop rent and profit all add cost
questions.expected: Factory processing, packaging, transport, shop rent and profit all add cost
questions.memo: Each step adds cost — and profit. The price reflects the whole chain, not just the raw material. This is normal but raises fair-trade questions.

questions.question: True or false: SA exports raw GOLD but doesn't always make the jewellery here.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: South Africa exports raw gold but doesn't always manufacture the jewellery here.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. SA earns less from raw gold than it would from finished jewellery. One challenge for SA is to manufacture more here — keep more of the value at home.

questions.question: Which is a way to support FAIR TRADE as a buyer?
questions.ruby_prompt: How can a buyer support fair trade?
options: Look for fair-trade labels and choose those products when possible
questions.expected: Look for fair-trade labels and choose those products when possible
questions.memo: Fair-trade labels show a product has been certified — farmers/workers got fair pay. It's one small thing buyers can do for a fairer world.

questions.question: True or false: Trade has been happening for THOUSANDS OF YEARS.
